av_event.what: She brings both hands up into frame and slowly rubs the knuckles of her right hand with her left thumb, flexing the stiff fingers, and her face tightens in a brief wince before the smile comes back.

text:
A: Hello! Hi, can you hear me? Sorry, I never know if I do this right, the button for the camera.
B: Yes, I can hear you fine. Hello. I'm Tariq.
A: Tariq, lovely. I'm Agnieszka. Erm, is difficult name, everybody here says Aga, is fine, you can say Aga.
B: Agnieszka. I'll try the full one, if that's okay.
A: Oh! Very good, very good, nobody does that. So how are you, you are okay? You did the puzzle thing before?
B: I did, yes. I'm well, thank you. The puzzle was, er, harder than I expected towards the end. I ran out of time on the last two.
A: Me too! I was like, oh my God, the clock, the clock. I get nervous with the tests, you know, I think somebody is watching me. My son he laugh at me, he says Mum, it's not exam.
B: How old is your son?
A: Kacper, he is seventeen, he does plumbing at college. Is good, plumber always has work, I tell him. And my daughter Natalia, she is twenty-one, she moved out last year to Eastleigh with boyfriend. So now is quiet in house, only my husband and Kacper and me. You have children?
B: Two. A son, seventeen as well, doing A-levels. And a daughter, fourteen.
A: Seventeen, same! Is hard age, no? They don't tidy, they don't talk, only phone.
B: Mine talks, but mostly to tell me revision is going fine. Which I, er, I have my doubts about.
A: Yes, yes, I know this! And what you do, for work? I thought from the picture, maybe teacher, or doctor.
B: No, nothing so noble. I'm a team leader at a contact centre in Stratford. Broadband and mobile. I look after eleven advisers, and I take the difficult calls when a customer wants someone more senior.
A: Oh, the angry people. I am sorry for you. I call once for my internet and I was forty minutes waiting with music.
B: That wasn't us, I hope. What do you do?
A: I'm cleaner, part-time. Offices and one GP surgery in city centre, in Southampton. I start at six in the morning, sometimes evenings also. Is okay, I like it, I like the reception girls, we talk. But in winter the early bus, oh, is freezing and always late, and is not good for my hands.
B: Six is early. I'd struggle with that.
A: You get used. Well, sort of. I would like maybe a school job, daytime, normal hours, you know. That is my dream, not big dream.
B: It sounds like a sensible one, to be honest. Predictable hours matter more than people think.
A: Yes! Exactly. And you, you live in London?
B: Ilford. East London. I've been in London about twenty-five years now. I came from Karachi originally.
A: Twenty-five! I am almost twenty, from Poland, near Rzeszów. You still feel, erm, like you are from there? Because me, sometimes I don't know. In Poland they say I'm English now, and here I'm Polish.
B: That's, er... yes. I think that's quite precise, actually. When I'm abroad I say I'm a Londoner. When I'm in London I'm Pakistani. It sort of depends who's asking, right?
A: Yes, who is asking! I like this. I will say this to my husband.
B: Do you go back often?
A: Every summer, two, three weeks. My mum is there, my sister. Mum is alone now since my dad died, so I call her every day, video, long calls. She shows me her garden. You go to Pakistan?
B: Every couple of years. For family. It's more duty than holiday, if I'm honest. When I want a holiday I'd rather go somewhere new. Granada, Istanbul. I spent a whole afternoon at the Alhambra just looking at ceilings.
A: Ceilings! Oh, you are the art person. Me, no, I am honest, museums I don't understand. I like my Polish series and the singing in church.
B: That's perfectly fair. Nobody needs to like ceilings.
A: My husband likes the ceiling only when it's not leaking! Oh, is it finishing? The timer?
B: I think so. It was nice to meet you, Agnieszka.
A: You too, you said my name very good! Bye, bye!
